semantics: CPU samples are observations, not function invocation counts. The samples/count decode and cpu-time decode agree on 10ms per sample.
Cumulative symbols in the same call chain overlap. Focus unions also overlap each other; never sum categories or nested cumulative rows.
The profiles account for about 0.40-0.42 sampled cores per service, not saturation of GOMAXPROCS=2. Ratios are sampled CPU/wall, not a host utilization measurement.

The 213-243ms barrier means, 11-13us snapshot means and 208 origin cohort_busy counts belong to the prior unprofiled run supplied by the parent. They are not per-request spans joined to these CPU samples.
Profiling is diagnostic and cannot qualify the unchanged unprofiled first-attempt or latency gate.
proven_facts: The largest sampled CPU chain on each node is generic transport writeLoop -> writeOutboundBatch -> WriteFramesInto -> net.Buffers.WriteTo -> writev: 450/410/540ms, 34.88/30.60/42.19 percent of sampled CPU. The fixed symbols do not separate Raft, RPC or channel traffic.
Pebble WAL flushLoop is visible at 60/90/90ms cumulative; syncWithLatency -> File.Sync is 20/20/30ms on the same chain. These generic symbols do not distinguish message, metadata or raftlog stores.
Slot Multi-Raft stack unions account for 40/20/30ms, mostly apply/metadata/snapshot paths. Metadata Apply/Commit stack unions account for 40/20/30ms. Neither is the dominant sampled CPU chain.
No CPU samples match the fixed explicit ReadBarrier/ReadIndex frame expression. Inbound quorum processing can execute in shared Raft Step code without these frames.
not_supported_or_narrowly_excluded: These samples do not support claiming sustained two-P CPU saturation, a ReadIndex busy-spin dominating CPU, or a WAL/fsync dominant on-CPU workload. They do not statistically exclude short bursts outside or inside the sampled interval.
A large percentage attributed to writev does not prove full CPU utilization, socket congestion, kernel wait duration, host contention or a permission critical-path bottleneck.
A small fsync CPU count cannot rule out long disk latency, serialized commit waits, or queueing behind other store commits.
unknowns: Breakdown of barrier elapsed time among waiting for the Slot worker/control turn, safe quorum confirmation, transport delay, durable apply, commit coordination and runnable scheduling.
Exact overlap between active origin cohorts, directory projector work, store-specific writes and a particular rejected SEND.

Whether Ready requeue fairness, directory completion head-of-line blocking, projector write amplification or host I/O/runnable contention is the material cause. CPU-only data cannot choose among these.

source_evidence.fact: Active cohorts are bounded at 64; ownership stays through synchronous fresh read/RPC work. Busy origin admission therefore can be amplified by elapsed I/O waiting without heavy permission CPU.
Fresh barrier precedes the permission snapshot; envelope and maintenance ownership remain held.
Barrier queues controlReadBarrier and then waits on a response or ctx, which CPU profiles do not measure as elapsed waiting.
A confirmed read still waits for durableAppliedIndex >= ReadIndex.
Ready processing can requeue before controls; this is a possible scheduling mechanism, not proof that it caused this run.
Ready persistence precedes transport sends and acceptReadStates; durable apply occurs on the ordered apply path.
Ready with HardState, entries or snapshot synchronously calls Storage.Save.
Metadata commits retain hash-slot locks through one durable terminal outcome; after locking they submit without caller cancellation and finalize by unlocking.
Commit coordinator uses engine Batch.Commit(true). This establishes a synchronous durability mechanism, not its measured wait time.
Generic outgoing frames are written through writeFramesInto using the raw connection.
net.Buffers.WriteTo is the sampled writev ancestor.
